'''''Pteris tremula''''', commonly known as '''Australian brake''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=PTTR3|taxon=Pteris tremula|accessdate=15 October 2015}}</ref> '''tender brake''', '''tender brakefern''', '''shaking brake''' is a [[fern]] [[species]] of the family [[Pteridaceae]] native to sheltered areas and forests in eastern [[Australia]] and [[New Zealand]]. It has pale green, lacy fronds of up to {{convert|2|m|ft|abbr=off|sp=us}} in length. It is fast-growing and easy to grow in cultivation, but can become weedy.

==Description==
''Pteris tremula'' is a terrestrial fern, with its [[frond]]s arising from the ground up to {{convert|1.3|m|ft|abbr=on}} with an erect, tufted [[rhizome]] that is covered with narrow brown scales, rarely up to {{convert|2|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall. The stipe is brown. The light green lacy compound fronds may reach {{convert|2|m|ft|abbr=on}} in length and are 3-pinnate or more. The brownish sori line the undersides of the frond margins.<ref name=plantnet>{{cite web|title=''Pteris tremula''|work= PlantNET - NSW Flora Online|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Pteris~tremula|accessdate=2010-06-27}}</ref> 

Unlike ''[[Pteris vittata]]'' and other ''Pteris'' species, it is not able to [[hyperaccumulate]] [[arsenic]] and is damaged by levels as low as 25 mg/kg in the soil.<ref>{{Cite journal| last1 = Wang | first1 = H.| last2 = Wong | first2 = M.| last3 = Lan | first3 = C.| last4 = Baker | first4 = A.| last5 = Qin | first5 = Y.| last6 = Shu | first6 = W.| last7 = Chen | first7 = G.| last8 = Ye | first8 = Z.| title = Uptake and accumulation of arsenic by 11 Pteris taxa from southern China| journal = Environmental Pollution| volume = 145| issue = 1| pages = 225–233| year = 2007| pmid = 16777301| doi = 10.1016/j.envpol.2006.03.015}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| last1 = Caille | first1 = N.| last2 = Zhao | first2 = F.| last3 = McGrath | first3 = S.| title = Comparison of root absorption, translocation and tolerance of arsenic in the hyperaccumulator Pteris vittata and the nonhyperaccumulator Pteris tremula| journal = The New Phytologist| volume = 165| issue = 3| pages = 755–761| year = 2005| pmid = 15720686| doi = 10.1111/j.1469-8137.2004.01239.x| doi-access = free}}</ref> The plant contains two [[cytotoxic]] indanonic [[sesquiterpene]]s.<ref>[http://www.sbras.ru/PSB/phsb/papers/CSD2002_04_1e.pdf Chlorine-Containing Sesquiterpenes of Higher Plants] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110718103755/http://www.sbras.ru/PSB/phsb/papers/CSD2002_04_1e.pdf |date=2011-07-18 }} Valery M. Dembitsky and Genrich A. Tolstikov ''Chemistry for Sustainable Development'' 10 (2002) 363–370</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The range within Australia is Central Australia (Northern Territory), eastern South Australia, Queensland, eastern New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania. It is also found on [[Lord Howe Island|Lord Howe]] and [[Norfolk Island]], New Zealand, and the [[Kermadec Islands]] and Fiji. It is found in sheltered habitats in wet sclerophyll and rainforest.<ref name=EJ02/> It has become naturalized in [[Argentina]] near the [[Río de la Plata]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Arana |first1=Marcelo Daniel |last2=Berrueta |first2=Pedro C. |last3=Gorrer |first3=Daniel |last4=Giudice |first4=Gabriela Elena |last5=Luna |first5=María Luján |title=''Pteris tremula'' (Polypodiopsida: Pteridaceae): A Naturalized Species in Argentina |journal=American Fern Journal |volume=110 |issue=2 |pages=66–69 |year=2020|doi=10.1640/0002-8444-110.2.66 |s2cid=218972896 |hdl=11336/136374 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Pteris tremula Raven Street Reserve Chermside West P1070232.jpg|thumb|In native habitat]]
''Pteris tremula'' is a fairly easy plant to grow in the home garden, where it prefers a shady spot.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Hambrett|first=Jo|date=August 2003|title=Summer iii – he garden|journal=Garden Design Study Group Newsletter|publisher=Australian Native Plants Society|issue=43|page=12|issn=1039-9062}}</ref> It prefers fair drainage with some moisture retention in the soil and filtered morning light. It is nevertheless fast growing and has been known to naturalise.<ref name=EJ02/> In the 1950s it was reported to be the most commonly cultivated ''Pteris'' species in the United States of America.<ref>{{Cite journal| last1 = Morton | first1 = C. V.| title = Observations on Cultivated Ferns. I| jstor = 1545392| journal = American Fern Journal| volume = 47| issue = 1| pages = 7–14| year = 1957| doi = 10.2307/1545392}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The botanist [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]] published this plant in the year 1810, in his ''[[Prodromus Florae Novae Hollandiae]]'', and still bears its original name.<ref>{{APNI | name = ''Pteris tremula'' R.Br.  | id = 18549}}</ref> The [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] ''tremula'' is the [[Latin]] "tremulous" or "shaking". It is a member of the large genus ''[[Pteris]]'', containing around 300 species, 7 of which can be found in Australia. ''Tender brake'' is a common name for the fern.<ref name=EJ02>{{cite book | last1=Elliot | first1=Rodger W. | last2=Jones | first2=David L. | last3=Blake | first3=Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation: Volume 8 – Pr-So|year=2002 |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne |isbn=0-7344-0378-X|pages=59–60}}</ref> Species in ''Pteris'' are currently placed in subfamily [[Pteridoideae]] of family [[Pteridaceae]]/<ref name=Christenhusz-2011 />
